questions.question: Why model the harness loop as an explicit state machine rather than a while loop with flags?
options: It runs measurably faster than an equivalent while loop because CPython optimizes named state transitions at the bytecode level
It removes the need for integration tests, since a state machine is correct by construction once the states are named
It lets the harness reject illegal transitions in one place and replay sessions from the event log
It is required because a language model can only emit tool calls when the caller exposes a formal state machine
questions.explanation: A state machine puts the legality rules in one transition function. The same input sequence reproduces the same state, which is what makes session replay possible. Speed, test coverage, and what a model can call are unrelated to why the shape was chosen.

questions.question: What does a pull point in the loop represent?
options: A model call inside PLANNING that returns the name of the next tool to invoke without yielding control
A wall-clock timer that fires on a fixed interval and forces a transition back to IDLE
A hook subscriber in before_tool_call that mutates the payload before dispatch and returns control
A point where the loop yields control back to the caller and waits for an input to resume
questions.explanation: Pull points are returns, not exceptions or timers. The caller fetches what the harness asked for and calls resume().

questions.question: Which state is the only legal pull point for a tool call?
options: EXECUTING — while the current step is actively running
AWAITING_TOOL — while blocked on a tool result
REFLECTING — right after a step's result comes back
PLANNING — while the next step's plan is drafted
questions.explanation: Only AWAITING_TOOL yields a tool pull point. EXECUTING transitions into it when a step requires a tool.

questions.question: What happens when a hook raises HookAbort in before_tool_call?
options: The tool call is skipped, on_error fires with the abort reason, and the loop moves to REFLECTING
The session immediately transitions to DONE without emitting a completion event, ending the run early
The hook that raised HookAbort is automatically unregistered so it cannot abort future tool calls
The budget envelope is reset to its initial turn, tool-call, and wall-clock limits so the run continues
questions.explanation: HookAbort cancels the in-flight tool dispatch, fires on_error with the abort reason, and continues into REFLECTING. It does not end the session, unregister the hook, or touch the budget.

questions.question: Why are hooks and events kept as separate concerns?
options: Because event types are serialized as raw bytes on disk while hooks are addressed by string names in the registry
Because a separate audit script forbids registering more than one subscriber per hook topic
Because the append-only event log cannot store Python dict payloads, only flat scalar values
Hooks are imperative and can mutate or abort execution. Events are observational and append-only.
questions.explanation: Hooks change behavior. Events describe behavior. Mixing them couples policy and telemetry, which is the bug we are avoiding — it has nothing to do with serialization format or subscriber counts.

questions.question: When the wall-clock budget is exceeded, what is the next state?
options: DONE — the session is terminated immediately, no further resume calls accepted
IDLE — a pull point returns with a budget_exceeded reason for the caller
EXECUTING — the loop silently retries the current step until the check passes
PLANNING — a fresh plan is drafted automatically using the remaining budget headroom
questions.explanation: Budget exhaustion is a yield, not a kill switch. The harness transitions to IDLE, fires on_budget_exceeded, and returns a PullRequest so the caller can decide whether to extend or close.

questions.question: Why does this lesson stub out the planner instead of calling a model?
options: To keep the loop contract testable and deterministic before any model or real planner is bound to it
Because local model calls add enough latency that the test suite would time out on typical CI hardware
Because a language model is structurally incapable of returning a tool-call payload from an API response
To save on token spend while iterating on the harness's internal state machine during development
questions.explanation: Pinning the loop contract first lets later lessons swap in real planners, registries, and dispatchers without renegotiating the state machine. Models return tool calls just fine — that is not the reason.
